name: chDB
summary: The ClickHouse engine packaged as a library: run ClickHouse SQL inside a Python, Go, Rust or Node.js program, with no server.
intro: chDB is ClickHouse compiled into a library that loads into your own process. A call such as `chdb.query(sql, "DataFrame")` goes straight into ClickHouse’s parser, planner and vectorised engine, with no server, socket or child process; the result comes back in any ClickHouse output format (CSV, JSON, Arrow, Parquet or a pandas DataFrame), handed to Python through a `memoryview` to avoid copying. By default it keeps nothing: tables live in memory and disappear with the process. Open a connection or session on a path and it keeps tables on disk in the same format as `clickhouse-local`, so the two can share a database directory. It reaches data where it sits through ClickHouse’s table functions, such as `file()`, `s3()`, `url()`, `mysql()` and `postgresql()`, and the `Python()` table function queries a pandas DataFrame or Arrow table in place.

The engine itself ships as `chdb-core` (26.9.0, September 2026), versioned like ClickHouse. The `chdb` Python package (4.4.0) sits on top and adds DataStore, a pandas-compatible API that records a chain of pandas calls and compiles it into one ClickHouse query when you ask for the result. Bindings exist for C/C++, Go, Rust, Node.js, Bun, Java, Ruby, .NET, Zig and WebAssembly, at very different stages of maturity. It is Apache 2.0 licensed and free; ClickHouse, Inc. took the project over in March 2024 and employs its creator. Version 4.4 adds `chdb.durable`, which keeps a database’s state in an S3, GCS or Azure bucket you own, with a lease that guarantees a single writer.
strengths: The full ClickHouse SQL dialect and function library from a `pip install`, with no server to run
Reads and writes 60+ formats, and queries S3, URLs, MySQL and PostgreSQL directly through ClickHouse table functions
SQL over pandas DataFrames and Arrow tables in place, or pandas-style code run on the engine through DataStore
The same SQL runs later on a ClickHouse server or ClickHouse Cloud, and on-disk databases are interchangeable with `clickhouse-local`
Apache 2.0, with a full-time team at ClickHouse, Inc.
limits: The Python package supports Linux and macOS only; there are no native Windows wheels
One process can have only one active data path: switching to a different on-disk database means closing the first
Outside Python, C/C++, Node.js and Go, the bindings are marked early or experimental in the project’s own capability matrix
Python UDFs are scalar only, receive every argument as a string and are called once per row
One machine and one process, like DuckDB: it isn’t a shared server for many users

snippet.title: SQL over Parquet on S3 and a pandas DataFrame, in one process
source: # ClickHouse SQL straight over Parquet files, returned as a DataFrame
SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, count() AS views
GROUP BY day ORDER BY day
# Join it with an in-memory DataFrame through the Python() table function
SELECT d.day, d.views, t.goal, d.views >= t.goal AS hit
FROM Python(daily) AS d JOIN Python(targets) AS t USING (day)
# Keep tables between runs: a session on a directory
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS clicks ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY ts AS

sections.title: chDB or DuckDB?
sections.intro: Both run analytical SQL inside your process with no server. The difference is mostly where the engine came from and where you can take your queries next.

story: ClickHouse had long shipped `clickhouse-local`, a single binary that runs SQL over local and remote files without a server. But data scientists live in Python, and calling a separate binary through pipes meant starting a process for every query and copying every result. In February 2023, Auxten Wang wanted to read large annotation datasets from a Jupyter notebook while training computer-vision models, without waiting on slow Hive clusters. Over the Lunar New Year he built a prototype that linked ClickHouse’s 900,000 lines of C++ straight into a Python module.

Lorenzo Mangani of QXIP soon joined, adding Go, Node.js and Rust bindings, and the projects moved to a chdb-io GitHub organisation. ClickHouse, Inc. promoted chDB in its 23.7 release call and an August 2023 blog post. In March 2024 it announced that chDB was now part of ClickHouse and that Auxten would work on it full-time, with chDB tracking ClickHouse releases. chDB 4, announced in March 2026, split the engine into `chdb-core` and added DataStore, aimed at people who write pandas rather than SQL.

choices.choice: Link the engine into the process instead of wrapping the binary
choices.why: Running `clickhouse-local` through pipes added 10 to 50 ms of process start per query, copied every result and ruled out Python UDFs and SQL on DataFrames.

choices.choice: Hand results over in memory, not through stdout
choices.why: Writing output into ClickHouse’s in-memory write buffer and exposing it through Python’s `memoryview` avoids copying results from C++ into Python objects.
A chDB database directory can be opened by `clickhouse-local` and vice versa, so data moves between the two without export.

timeline.text: Auxten Wang starts chDB in February; v0.1.0 in March, v1.0.0 in December
chDB becomes part of ClickHouse, Inc. in March
chDB 4 adds the pandas-compatible DataStore; the engine becomes `chdb-core`
September: durable storage on object stores and a PostgreSQL extension
